title: US firm AI investment is associated with recent productivity growth through organization capital
source_unit: US firm-level AI-skilled employment, job descriptions, organization capital, sales per worker, and productivity growth

observations.period: 2018–2024 compared with the prior decade; working paper issued August 2026

denominator.unit: US firm-level panel; exact firm-year count not disclosed in the NBER abstract

ai_investment_and_productivity.unit: AI investments are associated with productivity growth in recent years but not over the previous decade

organization_capital.unit: productivity gains are traced to durable firm-specific knowledge acquired through learning-by-doing

ai_skilled_jobs.unit: productivity gains are driven by AI-skilled jobs that build organization capital

workforce_composition_comparator.unit: related NBER workforce-composition evidence reports more educated, STEM-, and IT-intensive workforces, more junior workers, and fewer middle-management and senior workers as firms invest in AI

sales_per_worker_featured_estimate.unit: the existing project summary reports 6.2 percentage points greater 2018–2024 sales-per-worker growth for a one-standard-deviation increase in AI-skilled employment-share growth; the abstract does not reproduce this estimate

observations.method: Firm-level measure of AI investment based on AI-skilled employment, matched job-description measure of organization capital, and comparison of recent productivity growth with the prior decade.
observations.uncertainty: The paper is a working paper and the abstract describes associations, not a randomized or fully causal estimate. The abstract does not disclose firm counts, sector estimates, worker pay, job quality, or how broadly the constructed organization-capital measure transfers across firms.
observations.subgroup: US firms with different AI-skilled employment growth, job-description-based organization capital, sectors, and organizational learning capacity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Firms that already have stronger management, demand, capital, or workers may both hire AI-skilled workers and grow faster; AI-skilled employment can signal selection or complementary investment rather than the independent effect of AI.

related_sources.claim: Published NBER chapter evidence finds that AI-investing firms shift toward more educated, STEM-, and IT-intensive workforces, with more junior workers and fewer middle-management and senior workers.
US product-market rivalry and cost-of-capital shocks shape investment, markups, and concentration.
Worker heterogeneity explains much of the modeled variation in labor-supply elasticities and wage markdowns.
US product-market creative destruction passes asymmetric risk into incumbent-worker earnings and jobs.

boundary: This record adds a firm-performance signal to the AI-work chain. It does not establish that AI caused the productivity association, that workers received the gains, that job quality or control improved, or that consumers and households benefited.
